slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter sixteen: the examination of bondage and liberation.

slides.heading: Who is bound, and who is freed?
points: Beings bound in samsara, the round of birth and death
Someone tied up, wandering, one day set free
Who is that someone? What binds? What frees?
slides.say: Buddhism speaks of beings bound in samsara, the round of birth and death, and of liberation from it. The words suggest a picture: someone is tied up, wanders from life to life, and one day is set free. This chapter asks who that someone is, what binds them, and what it would mean to be released. It looks for the traveller, the rope and the moment of untying, and finds none of them standing on its own.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Carries on the search for the self of chapter 9
Uses the analysis of going from chapter 2
Leads into chapter 17 and prepares chapter 25
slides.say: The chapter carries forward the search for the self in chapter nine and the analysis of going in chapter two. It leads directly into chapter seventeen, on action and its fruit, and its last verse prepares the famous claim of chapter twenty-five, that samsara and nirvana are not two places.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Who wanders?
points: Samsara means 'wandering on'
If there is wandering, something must wander
First candidates: the formations, and a living being
slides.say: Now the explanation. Samsara literally means wandering on. If there is wandering, something must wander. Verse sixteen point one tries the most obvious candidates: the formations, the changing physical and mental events that make up a life, and the living being made of them.

slides.heading: Permanent or impermanent?
slides.say: Suppose the formations wander from one life to the next. Are they permanent or impermanent? A permanent thing cannot wander. To go from here to there is to change, and what is permanent does not change. An impermanent thing cannot wander either. It is gone the moment after it appears, so it never makes the journey. A wave does not carry the same water across the ocean. Wandering needs something that both stays the same, so that it is the one that wanders, and changes, so that it moves on. A thing with a fixed nature can do only one of the two. The same holds for a living being taken as a thing with its own nature: fixed, it cannot move on; momentary, it is not there to arrive.

slides.heading: Perhaps the person wanders
points: Verse 16.2: the person, not the passing events
Held by the Pudgalavadin schools
A person neither the same as nor different from the aggregates
slides.say: Perhaps it is the person who wanders, rather than the passing events. That is verse sixteen point two. Some early Buddhist schools, the Pudgalavadins, held exactly this: there is a person who is neither the same as the aggregates nor different from them, and it carries karma from life to life.

slides.heading: The fivefold search
slides.say: Nagarjuna answers with the fivefold search already set out with fire and fuel in chapter ten, which chapter twenty-two later applies to the Buddha himself. Look for the person in five ways. Is it the same as the aggregates: body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness? Is it different from them? Is it inside them? Are they inside it? Does it own them, as one owns a coat? Each answer fails. If the person were the aggregates, it would be as many as they are and would end when they end. If it were different, it could be found apart from them, and it never is. In, containing and owning all need two separate things, and the second thing is just what cannot be found. The same search can be run on the sense bases and the elements. Nowhere is there a someone to make the journey.

slides.heading: The gap between two lives
slides.say: Verse sixteen point three adds a sharper point. Grasping, or taking-up, is what keeps a life going: the body, the mind and the sense of self are taken up again and again. Suppose a being passes from one taking-up, this life, to the next. Between letting go of the first and taking up the second, what is it? At that point it has no body, no aggregates, nothing it has taken up. It would be without existence. And a being with no existence and nothing taken up is not anyone. A self that passes between lives would have to exist, for a while, with nothing it exists as. That is not a subtle self. It is no self at all.

slides.heading: Continuity without a traveller
points: One life is conditioned by another
But the link is not a traveller
Nagasena's flame: neither the same nor different
slides.say: This is not a denial that one life is conditioned by another. It is a denial that the link is a traveller. The books use Nagasena's image: the flame of the last watch of the night is neither the flame of the first watch nor a different flame, and nothing passes from one to the other. Continuity is real and designated. A carrier is not found.

slides.heading: Then who is bound, and who is freed?
points: 16.4: nirvana makes no sense for fixed things
16.5: what arises and passes is not bound or freed
16.6: grasping binds neither grasper nor non-grasper
slides.say: If no one is found to wander, the same difficulty meets the goal. Verse sixteen point four says that nirvana makes no sense for the formations or for a being, taken as things with their own nature. A momentary event is gone before it could be liberated. A permanent self could never change its state from bound to free. Verse sixteen point five says the same about bondage: events that arise and pass away have nothing lasting in them to be held and then released. Verses six to eight look at the bond itself, with the same pattern chapter two used for going. Say the bond is grasping. Is the one bound by it already grasping, or not? If already grasping, already bound, the bond has nothing to add. If not grasping, it is not bound. There is no third state in which the binding takes place. A bond would have to exist before the one it binds, as a rope exists before the hands it ties. But grasping is not found apart from the one who grasps. For the rest, verse sixteen point seven simply points back to chapter two's analysis of gone, not gone and going.

slides.heading: Bound, unbound, being freed
slides.say: Release has the same shape, says verse sixteen point eight. One who is bound is not, as bound, free. One who is not bound has nothing to be freed from. And to be being freed while still bound would put bondage and release at the same moment. Release pictured as a self-standing person passing from a self-standing state of bondage to a self-standing state of freedom has no place to happen.

slides.heading: The great grasping
points: 'Free of grasping, I shall reach nirvana'
'Nirvana will be mine'
Nagarjuna: a great hold of grasping
slides.say: Verse sixteen point nine turns from logic to practice, and it is the heart of the chapter. Free of grasping, I shall reach nirvana; nirvana will be mine. This sounds like the very attitude a practitioner should have. Nagarjuna calls it a great hold of grasping. The reason is simple once seen. The sentence keeps everything that liberation was meant to release: an I who will arrive, a nirvana that will be mine, a future state to be acquired and kept. It turns the path into a project of the self. The more earnestly it is held, the tighter the hold. This does not mean practice is useless, or that one should not aspire. It means that what frees is the seeing that the one who grasps and the thing grasped are not found as they are taken to be, not a better object for the same grasping.

slides.heading: Nothing added, nothing removed
points: Nirvana is not added on, like a prize
Samsara is not taken away, like a stain
What ends is the construction that made them two
slides.say: The last verse, sixteen point ten, says what is left. Liberation is not adding nirvana to a being, like a prize, and it is not taking samsara away, like a stain. If nothing is added and nothing removed, what samsara is there, and what nirvana is being conceived as its opposite? Chandrakirti reads this as the point of the chapter: since bondage and liberation are both empty, there is no samsara to be cut off and no nirvana to be gained as a separate thing. What ends is the conceptual construction that built them into two places. Chapter twenty-five will say it in its boldest form: there is not the slightest difference between the two.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Suffering is real as lived, and it has causes
When grasping ends, the round ends
What goes: a traveller, a rope, an untying
slides.say: The chapter does not say that no one suffers, or that practice makes no difference. Suffering is real as it is lived, and it has causes. Grasping is what keeps the round going, and when grasping ends, the round ends. All of this holds as dependent arising. What the chapter removes is the picture of a self-standing someone who wanders, wears a self-standing rope and is one day untied. Ordinary language keeps working: she was freed from that fear is true, and the path is walked. It is walked well when it is not held as the journey of a traveller toward a possession. The companion book puts it plainly: conventional reality never required liberation from ontology; only conceptual thought did.

slides.heading: In the books
points: The Logic of Dependency: 'A Different Path'
Substrateless World: Chapter 9 and the Interlude
Anatta to Emptiness: The Last Refuge; Beyond the Extremes
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, in its section A Different Path, shows how the path, pictured as a traveller moving toward a goal, hardens into grasping. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter nine, on the problem of the invariant bearer, and the Interlude, on nirvana as this world no longer misread. In The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness: The Last Refuge of Ontology, and Beyond the Extremes, where no subject who was bound and is now free survives the analysis. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter seventeen, the examination of actions and their fruits.
